Four laboratory-confirmed deaths have occurred in Ituri province; suspected cases have also been reported in Bunia, a city of nearly 700,000. Risks are heightened by mining-driven population movements, insecurity, and gaps in contact tracing, along with proximity to Uganda and South Sudan. articleHeadline: Thailand Lists Hantavirus as Dangerous Disease
articleSummary: Nonthaburi, Thailand—Thailand's National Communicable Disease Committee (NCDC) designates hantavirus infection as a dangerous communicable disease, adding hantavirus to the 14th high-alert disease on the national list. Stricter surveillance requires suspected cases to be reported within 3 hours and investigations to begin within 12 hours; high-risk contacts are quarantined for 42 days from last exposure. The designation covers Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS) and Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS). Transmission concerns include respiratory droplets and potential person-to-person spread for some strains. Measures include enhanced entry-point surveillance with formal PUI criteria, rapid-response protocols, 42-day quarantines, lab upgrades at the Department of Medical Sciences, nationwide treatment and infection-control guidelines, and intensified provincial surveillance and risk communications. Public advice: rodent exposure or travel to high-risk areas with fever or breathing difficulties warrants prompt medical care and disclosure of travel history.

The majority of cases and deaths are in Mongwalu and Rwampara health zones, with four deaths among laboratory-confirmed cases. Suspected cases in Bunia are pending laboratory confirmation. Ebola virus disease is highly contagious and spreads through bodily fluids such as vomit, blood, or semen; the disease is severe and often fatal. The new outbreak follows five months after Congo's last Ebola outbreak was declared over, which caused 43 deaths. Ituri is a remote region with poor road networks, more than 1,000 kilometers from Kinshasa. The country has been battling armed groups in the east, including the M23 rebel group, complicating outbreak response.

articleHeadline: Pakar Unair Surabaya Ungkap Risiko Hantavirus di Tengah Mobilitas Global
articleSummary: Suspected hantavirus cluster aboard cruise ship MV Hondius triggers global health concern as passengers report severe respiratory distress. Indonesian epidemiologist Laura Navika Yamani of Universitas Airlangga, Surabaya, notes hantavirus can cause severe pneumonia with fatality rates of 30-50% in some cases. The incubation period spans weeks, so new cases may appear after travelers relocate, complicating outbreak investigations. Transmission occurs mainly via inhalation of aerosolized particles from urine, feces, or saliva of infected rodents; human-to-human spread is uncommon, though Andes virus has demonstrated limited transmission. The mobility of international travel and eco-tourism increases exposure risk, and environmental changes may alter rodent reservoirs. Clinical onset is non-specific at first—fever, fatigue, and gastrointestinal symptoms—progressing to severe respiratory failure. Emphasis on epidemiological tracing is crucial to identify infection sources and track potential imported or exported cases during cross-border voyages.

articleSummary: On 12 May 2026, at Government House, Bangkok, Thailand, the Department of Disease Control announced nationwide expansion of the pneumococcal vaccination (PCV) for all children, with full coverage in FY2027. The PCV schedule is three doses at 2, 4, and 12 months, designed to reduce pneumococcal disease—pneumonia, meningitis, and bacteremia—especially in children under 2 and the elderly, with Thai children experiencing more than 7,000 pneumococcal pneumonia cases annually. The policy also accelerates hepatitis B and C elimination. Thailand has about 1 million chronically HBV-infected and roughly 230,000 HCV-infected people. HBV vaccination prevents infection; HCV is curable with timely diagnosis and treatment. Screening expansions target those born before 1992 and high-risk groups, aiming to screen at least 30 million people (~80% of the target population) by 2028, alongside education and counseling to promote uptake.

articleSummary: Four-year-old boy in Vietnam (Central Dermatology Hospital, Hanoi) developed simultaneous herpes zoster (shingles) and chickenpox due to Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV). Initial painful vesicles and a linear cluster on the right thorax progressed to widespread vesicles on face, limbs, and trunk with fever 38–39°C. The patient, previously healthy with no immunodeficiency and HIV negative, was up to date with national vaccines except for varicella. Maternal chickenpox occurred during pregnancy. Two lesion cytology samples showed atypical squamous cells and multinucleated giant cells. Liver and kidney function were normal. Diagnosed with concurrent zoster and chickenpox; treated with oral acyclovir and supportive care. After 2 days, fever resolved, chest/back lesions improved, and no new lesions appeared. Literature notes similar cases in Iran, China, and Bangladesh; possible mechanism involves VZV latency and simultaneous reactivation. Emphasizes varicella vaccination and awareness of potential complications from shingles.

articleSummary: Ebola outbreak confirmed in Ituri province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, with about 246 suspected cases and 65 deaths reported as of 15 May 2026. The African CDC says the situation is being actively monitored and an expert emergency meeting has been convened to coordinate the response. The largest clusters are in Mongbwalu and Rwampara, while Bunia city faces elevated risk due to high population density and heavy human movement. Preliminary laboratory analyses suggest the outbreak is caused by an Ebola virus strain not belonging to Zaire ebolavirus; complete sequencing is underway to define its genetic structure. Transmission occurs via direct contact with bodily fluids of infected people, contaminated objects, or contact with the bodies of the deceased. Mining-related mobility in Mongbwalu may facilitate spread to larger areas, underscoring the need for rapid containment and public health measures.

articleHeadline: The politics of immobility in the British Empire Bombay and plague, c. 1896-1903
articleSummary: Bombay experienced a serious plague epidemic beginning in 1896, triggering panic in India and abroad. articleSummary: A new HIV-1 recombinant strain, CRF161_0107, was identified in Yunnan Province, Southwest China, by the local CDC team and published in Virologica Sinica. Genomic analysis shows a mosaic of CRF01_AE and CRF07_BC, with five recombination breakpoints dividing the genome into six alternating segments, indicating a stable, second-generation circulating recombinant form rather than a transient product. Molecular clock analysis places emergence around 2016, with several years of human transmission implying established spread. Phylogenetic tracing reveals a cross-regional origin: CRF01_AE?C5 fragment linked to northern China’s CRF01_AE?C5 lineage, and the CRF07_BC?N fragment derived from CRF07_BC?N. This marks the southwest China’s first report of CRF01_AE?C5-involved recombination, highlighting MSM mobility as a driver of inter-regional viral mixing and new strains. The study underscores the need for expanded molecular surveillance, integrating behavior interventions and informing vaccine and antiretroviral resistance monitoring.

articleSummary: In 2025, Brazil recorded 105,873 deaths from influenza and pneumonia and 2,550 deaths from coronavirus, with Roraima reporting 245 influenza/pneumonia deaths and 1 coronavirus death. articleSummary: First mainland Australian detection of the invasive Aedes albopictus, nicknamed the 'Barbecue Blocker,' found near Bamaga on the Cape York Peninsula, about 750 km northwest of Cairns. Six individuals (three males, three females) were identified during routine surveillance, far from typical entry ports. Aedes albopictus is a day-biting mosquito capable of transmitting dengue fever and Japanese encephalitis. Public health authorities say there is currently no virus detected in the captured mosquitoes and no active outbreak, but they are conducting large-scale spraying on the Cape York Peninsula and advising residents to reduce breeding sites. Origin remains unknown; possible links to recent illegal foreign fishermen are considered, with genetic analysis planned to determine source and whether it relates to earlier Torres Strait invasions (circa 2004–2005) of Indonesian origin. Protective measures: wearing long sleeves, using repellents, screens, and eliminating standing water.

articleSummary: May 15, 2026: West Java confirms hantavirus detected, among nine Indonesian provinces reporting rodent-borne viral infections. Karawang Regency Health Department says no hantavirus cases locally, but authorities have tightened surveillance for potential spread after reports in other West Java areas. Hantavirus is a zoonosis transmitted by rats via urine, feces, and saliva, and can also spread through dust contaminated with rodent excreta. Incubation ranges from 1–8 weeks depending on type. Clinically, two forms: Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS) affecting kidneys; and Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS), which affects the lungs and carries a high fatality rate (~60%). Early symptoms include fever, headache, body aches; HPS may cause acute shortness of breath. No specific antiviral exists; management is supportive. Diagnosis relies on laboratory confirmation (PCR or sequencing). Karawang follows the Ministry of Health’s alert directive for heightened vigilance.

articleSummary: Dengue infection in children is not inherently more susceptible than in adults, but they face higher mosquito exposure and can deteriorate faster once infected. In the monsoon and post-monsoon months, outdoor activity, greater skin exposure, and higher body heat/CO2 output lead to more Aedes bites, a factor that, along with a possibly differing skin bacterial profile, increases exposure. Severe dengue can progress in children because of smaller circulating blood volume; even plasma leakage may trigger shock and hemodynamic instability. Early recognition is challenging, as younger children may not articulate abdominal pain, vomiting, lethargy, or reduced urine. Parents should seek medical evaluation if fever is accompanied by persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, bleeding, rash, breathing difficulty, or irritability. articleHeadline: CRISPR-based environmental detection of Burkholderia pseudomallei identifies sanitation gaps and melioidosis risk in northeast Thailand - Nature Communications
articleSummary: CRISPR-BEEPs, a CRISPR-based environmental assay for Burkholderia pseudomallei, enables sensitive melioidosis risk mapping in northeast Thailand. Compared with conventional culture-based plate inspection using double-qPCR as reference, CRISPR-BEEPs showed 93.5% sensitivity and 100% specificity versus 19.4% sensitivity and 98.0% specificity for culture-based methods. The study sampled water across 15,118 km2 in northeast Thailand, focusing on households of 439 melioidosis patients, 190 with other bacterial infections, and 506 healthy controls. CRISPR-BEEPs detected B. pseudomallei in groundwater (73.3%), surface water (32.9%), and piped water (26.2%), with results matching double-qPCR. Importantly, environmental detection within 10 km of households correlated with higher melioidosis risk (odds ratio 2.74; 95% CI 1.38–5.48), an association not discernible with standard methods. Findings expose sanitation gaps and support high-resolution environmental surveillance for disease prevention.

articleSummary: Brazilian neurologists warn of neurological syndromes linked to dengue, notably Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), even as dengue cases decline. From January to April 11 this year, about 230,000 probable dengue cases were recorded, roughly 75% fewer than the ~1 million in the same period in 2025. The drop reflects awareness campaigns, risk guidance, expanded immunization, and the Wolbachia strategy reducing transmission in Aedes aegypti in some Brazilian states and municipalities. Yet vigilance remains essential. Experts emphasize severe post-infection neurological complications, with GBS typically beginning in the feet and legs and potentially affecting breathing; symptoms can include pain, numbness, and reduced mobility, necessitating rapid diagnosis and treatment. Encephalitis and myelitis can also follow arbovirus infections. Estimated risk is 35–40 Guillain-Barré cases per million dengue infections, highest within 15 days post-infection. Ongoing prevention and early care are crucial; Zika and Chikungunya can also trigger serious neurological outcomes.

articleHeadline: Molecular characterization of Echinococcus granulosus sensu lato genotypes circulating in small ruminants in north India - Scientific Reports
articleSummary: In north India, 1049 slaughtered small ruminants from Chandigarh (314), Himachal Pradesh (394), and Haryana (341) were inspected for hydatid cysts; 85 were cyst-positive (Chandigarh 53, Himachal Pradesh 17, Haryana 15). Molecular typing of cyst material using mitochondrial cox I and ATP6 genes identified genotypes G1 and G3 of Echinococcus granulosus sensu stricto and genotype G6 of E. canadensis. Authorities report 246 suspected cases and 65 deaths. Africa CDC confirmed Ebola virus in Ituri; sequencing underway to characterize the strain. Of 20 samples tested in Kinshasa, four deaths were linked to the virus. Cases are centered in Mongbwalu and Rwampara health zones (each ~150,000 residents); suspected cases in Bunia (~300,000). Initial analyses suggest a non-Zaire ebolavirus; Zaïre strain has approved vaccines and treatments. OMS and MSF teams are on the ground. First burials have occurred; locals report cascading deaths—up to five to six per day in Mongbwalu. Healthcare workers lack PPE, and transport medicine supply is constrained. Ebola transmission via bodily fluids; incubation up to 21 days; symptoms fever, vomiting, bleeding, diarrhoea.

articleSummary: Ebola virus disease outbreak declared in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo’s Ituri province, with fatalities surpassing 60; latest totals reach 65 deaths, four laboratory-confirmed. Preliminary testing at Kinshasa’s National Biomedical Research Institute showed Ebola virus in 13 of 20 samples; further tests to identify the strain are underway. Cases and probable infections are concentrated in Mongwalu and Rwampara mining towns, with new suspected cases reported from Bunia, Ituri’s capital. Africa CDC plans a regional coordination meeting with the DRC, Uganda, South Sudan, and international partners to align response measures and cross-border surveillance. The outbreak heightens risk due to urban density, mining activity, and substantial cross-border movement. Transmission occurs via direct contact with infected body fluids or broken skin; early symptoms include vomiting, diarrhea, rashes and bleeding. No proven antiviral; WHO cites about 50% case fatality. The 2018–2020 outbreak remains the deadliest on record for the country.

articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in eastern Ituri province, Democratic Republic of Congo, with 246 cases and 65 deaths reported by Africa CDC, concentrated in the mining towns of Mongwalu and Rwampara. Africa CDC will convene officials from DRC, Uganda, South Sudan, and international partners to set response priorities and cross-border surveillance. Preliminary INRB tests in Kinshasa detected Ebola in 13 of 20 samples; further work is ongoing to identify the exact viral strain. Of the 65 deaths, four are laboratory-confirmed. Additional suspected cases in Bunia, the provincial capital, await laboratory confirmation. Transmission is via direct contact with bodily fluids; early symptoms include fever, muscle pain, fatigue, and sore throat, followed by vomiting, diarrhea, rash, and bleeding. No proven treatment; mortality around 50%. Authorities warn of high spread risk in urban and mining settings, underscoring the need for regional coordination. The government has not officially declared an epidemic; a press conference is expected.

articleHeadline: Na vzhodu DR Kongo razglasili izbruh ebole
articleSummary: As of May 15, 2026, Ebola outbreak declared in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (Ituri province). Africa CDC (AU) confirms four deaths with about 65 suspected deaths and more than 200 infections reported. Cross-border risk to Uganda and South Sudan prompts an emergency meeting among DR Congo, Uganda, South Sudan and partners to strengthen cross-border surveillance, preparedness, and response. This is the 17th Ebola outbreak in DRC since the virus’ discovery in 1976; the last outbreak in August in central DRC caused 34 deaths. Early laboratory results indicate the current outbreak is caused by a different Ebola virus strain than the Zaire ebolavirus, with definitive strain identification expected within 24 hours. Ebola virus causes hemorrhagic fever, is highly contagious, and spreads via contact with body fluids; main symptoms include high fever, vomiting, diarrhea, and bleeding.
